stem: A patient stops taking a drug. About how many half-lives until it is roughly 97% eliminated?
why: A drug is roughly 97% eliminated after about 5 half-lives (3.125% remains).

whys.B: After 2 half-lives, 75% is eliminated.
whys.C: Far more than needed.
whys.D: After 3 half-lives, 87.5% is eliminated.
whys.E: After 1 half-life, 50% is eliminated.

takeaway: 5 half-lives ≈ 97% gone.

stem: A patient on a CYP3A4 substrate starts a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. What should you watch for clinically?

options.A: Higher oral bioavailability of the inhibitor
options.B: Faster renal clearance of the substrate
options.C: Loss of effect from falling substrate levels
options.D: A shorter half-life of the substrate
options.E: Signs of toxicity from rising substrate levels

why: Inhibiting the CYP that clears the substrate raises its level — always check CYP interactions before adding a drug; one of the most preventable causes of toxicity.

whys.A: The concern is the substrate's level.
whys.B: Inhibition slows metabolic clearance.
whys.C: Falling levels follow an inducer.
whys.D: Slower clearance prolongs, not shortens, half-life.

takeaway: Inhibitor added → watch for substrate toxicity.
discriminator: The FIRST drug (substrate) is the one at risk.

stem: Before allopurinol, a patient tests positive for HLA-B*5801. Why does it matter?

options.B: Sharply higher risk of severe hypersensitivity
options.C: Predicts faster CYP2D6 metabolism of the drug
options.E: Has no bearing on drug selection here

why: HLA-B*5801 is associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol — a textbook pharmacogenomic screening consideration.

whys.A: It flags hypersensitivity risk, not absorption.
whys.C: HLA alleles relate to hypersensitivity.
whys.D: That is TPMT deficiency.
whys.E: It is a key screening consideration.

takeaway: HLA-B*5801 + allopurinol = severe hypersensitivity.
discriminator: HLA = hypersensitivity; CYP = metabolism; TPMT = thiopurine toxicity.

stem: A hospitalized patient receives a drug intravenously. Why is the bioavailability of this dose 100%?

options.A: The whole dose enters the bloodstream directly
options.B: IV drugs are always more potent than oral
options.C: IV drugs avoid all protein binding in plasma
options.D: IV drugs have the longest half-lives of all
options.E: IV drugs are never metabolized by the liver

why: IV has 100% bioavailability by definition — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly; there is no absorption step.

whys.B: Potency is a PD property, not bioavailability.
whys.C: Protein binding affects free drug, not bioavailability.
whys.D: Half-life is unrelated to bioavailability.
whys.E: IV drugs are still metabolized; they skip absorption and first-pass.

takeaway: F = fraction reaching systemic circulation unchanged; IV = 100%.
discriminator: No absorption phase → nothing lost → F = 100%.

stem: A patient's drug has a very high calculated volume of distribution (Vd). What does this suggest?

options.A: Rapid renal clearance of the drug
options.B: A large real anatomic space for the drug
options.C: High oral bioavailability of the drug
options.D: Most of the drug remains in plasma
options.E: Extensive distribution of drug into tissues

why: Vd relates total drug in the body to plasma concentration; a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.

whys.A: Vd describes distribution, not clearance.
whys.B: Vd is theoretical, not a real anatomic space.
whys.C: Bioavailability is the fraction reaching circulation.
whys.D: High Vd means the drug is mostly in tissue.

takeaway: High Vd = drug sequestered in tissue (e.g., digoxin).
discriminator: Vd is a calculated, theoretical volume — not anatomy.

stem: Which statement about the order of metabolism phases is correct?

options.A: Phase II must always follow Phase I
options.B: Phase II occurs only in the kidney
options.C: Phase I always follows Phase II
options.D: Phase I often comes first, but not always

why: Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always — some drugs go straight to conjugation.

whys.A: Some drugs go straight to conjugation.
whys.B: The phases are defined by reaction type, not organ.
whys.C: Phase I often comes BEFORE Phase II.
whys.E: Not every drug needs Phase I.

takeaway: Order is usual, not mandatory.
discriminator: Watch for 'always' in options about metabolism order.

stem: Which parameter most directly determines the time to reach steady state?
why: Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life.

whys.B: Route doesn't set time to steady state.
whys.C: Steady state takes 4–5 half-lives regardless of dose.
whys.D: Bioavailability is the fraction reaching circulation.
whys.E: Names have no PK effect.

takeaway: Half-life sets the clock for steady state.
discriminator: Dose size changes the level, not the time to get there.

stem: Which statement matches the lecture's personalized-pharmacotherapy model?

options.A: Genotype is irrelevant at steady state
options.B: Genotype alone should decide the drug
options.C: Genotype affects ADRs but not metabolism
options.D: Genotype is one input among several
options.E: Genotype matters only for IV drugs

why: Pharmacogenomics is one input among several — genotype, phenotype, disease state, and other medications combine into individualized therapy.

whys.A: Nothing limits genotype's relevance this way.
whys.B: Genotype alone never dictates therapy.
whys.C: It can alter metabolism (e.g., CYP activity).
whys.E: Variation alters metabolism, transport, targets, and response.

takeaway: Genotype + phenotype + disease + other meds.
discriminator: Never let one input decide therapy alone.

stem: A patient takes a large, highly protein-bound drug. Which elimination route did the lecture call important for such drugs?
why: Bile/feces: important for some large or protein-bound drugs.

whys.A: The lungs eliminate volatile agents.
whys.B: A minor route.
whys.C: The kidney is the dominant route for MOST drugs.
whys.E: A minor route that matters in lactation.

takeaway: Large or protein-bound → bile.
discriminator: Most drugs → kidney; large/bound → bile; volatile → lungs.

stem: On number lines, a narrow-TI drug's ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ sit close together. What is the implication?

options.A: The wide-TI drug is more likely toxic
options.B: A small error can move effective to toxic
options.C: TI has no real bearing on dosing safety
options.D: The drug must have a lower Emax overall
options.E: The drug is safer because it needs less

why: The ED₅₀–TD₅₀ gap is the TI; a narrow gap means a small dosing error can push a patient from effective to toxic.

whys.A: A wide TI means a large margin — generally safer.
whys.C: TI is exactly the effective-to-toxic margin.
whys.D: TI says nothing about Emax.
whys.E: A narrow TI means a SMALLER safety margin.

takeaway: Narrow gap = small margin = monitor closely.
discriminator: Distance between the markers IS the therapeutic index.

stem: Years after approval, a drug's label gains a new warning based on reports clinicians submitted to FDA MedWatch. What is MedWatch?

options.C: An FDA Phase III trial registry
options.D: An FDA dose-finding Phase I program

why: Adverse-event reporting: ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.

whys.A: Repurposing is a drug source, not a reporting system.
whys.C: Phase III is a pre-approval trial; MedWatch collects postapproval reports.
whys.D: Phase I is safety/dose-finding in healthy volunteers.
whys.E: MedWatch is about safety signals, not names.

takeaway: Postapproval safety signals come from adverse-event reporting.
discriminator: MedWatch = reporting after approval; Phases I–III = before approval.

stem: A PA reviews indication, contraindications, renal/hepatic function, interactions, and monitoring before prescribing. What is this?

options.D: Therapeutic index testing of the drug

why: This checklist is the clinical decision-making framework from 'Putting It All Together.'

whys.A: Receptors are one stop on the pathway.
whys.B: Phase IV is after approval, population-level.
whys.C: PGx is one input, not the whole checklist.
whys.D: TI compares toxic vs. effective doses.

takeaway: The checklist = the clinical decision-making framework.
discriminator: Individual prescribing decision → framework; population safety → Phase IV.

stem: Which reactions belong to Phase I (functionalization) metabolism?
why: Phase I — functionalization: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; primarily by CYP450 enzymes.

whys.A: These are Phase II conjugation reactions.
whys.B: Sulfation is Phase II.
whys.C: Methylation and glutathione conjugation are Phase II.
whys.D: Acetylation and glucuronidation are Phase II.

takeaway: Phase I = oxidize, reduce, hydrolyze.
discriminator: Any '-ation' conjugation (glucuronid-, sulf-, acetyl-, methyl-) is Phase II.

stem: A patient receives an IV drug. Which tissues will the drug reach most slowly?
why: Highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).

whys.A: Highly perfused — they receive drug fastest.
whys.B: Highly perfused — they receive drug fastest.
whys.C: Highly perfused — they receive drug fastest.
whys.E: Fat is slow, but the heart is highly perfused and receives drug fast.

takeaway: Poor perfusion = slow delivery: fat, bone.
discriminator: Perfusion, not distance, sets distribution speed.

stem: Which receptor subtypes are listed under the receptor target class?

options.B: Plasma-protein, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear
options.C: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, DNA
options.D: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, transporter-linked, nuclear
options.E: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear

why: Receptors: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear.

whys.A: The list says ligand-gated ion channel, not voltage-gated.
whys.B: Plasma proteins bind drug in plasma; G-protein-coupled is listed.
whys.C: DNA is under nucleic acids; nuclear receptors are listed.
whys.D: The list says enzyme-linked, not transporter-linked.

takeaway: Four receptor subtypes: GPCR, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear.
discriminator: Watch single-word swaps: ligand-gated (not voltage-gated), enzyme-linked, nuclear.

stem: A patient needs a rapid local effect in the lungs while minimizing systemic exposure. Which route fits?
why: Inhaled: rapid local effect in the lungs; minimizes systemic exposure for some drugs.

whys.A: IV is systemic, immediate, and 100% bioavailable.
whys.C: Topical gives a local effect at the application site.
whys.D: Transdermal gives slow, sustained SYSTEMIC absorption.
whys.E: IM is systemic and good for depot forms.

takeaway: Inhaled = lungs; topical = skin site; transdermal = systemic via skin.
discriminator: Transdermal is systemic; topical is local — a classic mix-up.

stem: A CKD patient takes a renally cleared, narrow-TI drug without dose adjustment. Which two changes occur?
why: Reduced renal clearance raises drug concentration and prolongs half-life.

whys.A: Half-life is prolonged when clearance falls.
whys.B: Both rise.
whys.D: CKD DECREASES clearance.
whys.E: Reduced clearance does the opposite.

takeaway: Clearance ↓ → t½ ↑ → concentration ↑.
discriminator: Both move UP together when clearance falls.

stem: A trial enrolls a few hundred patients with the target condition to estimate preliminary efficacy and side effects. Which phase is this?
why: Phase II = preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile in a few hundred patients with the target condition.

whys.A: Phase I uses a small group of healthy volunteers for safety and dosing.
whys.C: Phase III uses hundreds to thousands, often multi-site, to confirm efficacy.
whys.D: Phase IV follows the general prescribed population after approval.
whys.E: FDA review is a regulatory step, not a trial phase.

takeaway: Phase II = first look at whether it works, in patients.
discriminator: 'Few hundred patients' and 'preliminary' point to Phase II; 'confirm at scale' points to III.

stem: Which is NOT one of the lecture's purposes of drug metabolism?

options.A: Increasing a drug's lipid solubility for storage
options.B: Producing an active metabolite that extends effect
options.D: Inactivating an active drug for excretion
options.E: Activating a prodrug into its active form

why: Metabolism inactivates drugs, activates prodrugs, makes active metabolites, and occasionally toxic metabolites — it makes drugs easier to excrete, not more lipid-soluble for storage.

whys.B: Listed: active metabolite contributes to or extends effect.
whys.C: Listed: occasionally a toxic metabolite.
whys.D: Listed: inactivate to make excretion easier.
whys.E: Listed: activate a prodrug.

takeaway: Four purposes: inactivate, activate prodrug, active metabolite, toxic metabolite.
discriminator: Metabolism trends toward excretion (water-soluble), not storage.

stem: A patient about to start azathioprine has TPMT deficiency. What is the main concern?

options.A: Faster CYP2D6 metabolism and lost effect
options.B: No concern, since genotype never matters
options.C: Increased toxicity risk from the thiopurine
options.E: Severe HLA-linked hypersensitivity to the drug

why: TPMT deficiency raises toxicity risk with thiopurine drugs (e.g., azathioprine).

whys.A: CYP2D6 affects antidepressants and opioids.
whys.B: Genotype is one input among several — it still matters.
whys.D: Reduced activation is the CYP2C19–clopidogrel example.
whys.E: That is the HLA-B*5801–allopurinol example.

takeaway: TPMT ↓ → thiopurine toxicity ↑.
discriminator: TPMT pairs with thiopurines only.

stem: Which statement about lipid solubility and distribution is correct?

options.A: Lipophilic drugs cannot enter fatty tissue
options.B: Lipophilic drugs stay mainly within plasma
options.C: Lipophilic drugs cross membranes and enter fat
options.D: Polar drugs cross membranes most readily
options.E: Lipid solubility has no effect on spread

why: Lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.

whys.A: They distribute INTO fatty tissue.
whys.B: Lipophilic drugs cross membranes and distribute into fatty tissue.
whys.D: Polar drugs cross poorly.
whys.E: It is one of the four listed distribution factors.

takeaway: Lipophilic = crosses membranes, goes to fat.
discriminator: Lipid solubility matters for membranes, the BBB, and renal reabsorption alike.

stem: Which two factors reduce oral bioavailability?

options.B: High lipid solubility and tissue perfusion
options.E: First-pass metabolism and a high Vd

why: Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.

whys.A: Renal excretion is elimination after the drug is in circulation.
whys.B: These affect distribution, not oral bioavailability.
whys.C: Protein binding is distribution, not bioavailability.
whys.E: Vd describes distribution, not the fraction absorbed.

takeaway: Oral F < 100% because of absorption + first pass.
discriminator: Bioavailability is about what reaches circulation — not what happens after.

stem: Which statement about potency and efficacy is correct?

options.A: Higher potency always means higher efficacy
options.B: Efficacy is the dose needed for effect
options.C: A lower EC₅₀ means a lower potency
options.E: Potency matters more than efficacy clinically

why: Potency and efficacy are independent properties — a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.

whys.A: A drug can be very potent but have low efficacy.
whys.B: That is potency; efficacy is the maximal effect.
whys.C: Lower EC₅₀ = MORE potent.
whys.E: Efficacy matters much more clinically.

takeaway: Never infer efficacy from potency.
discriminator: Potency alone never tells you whether a drug 'works better.'

stem: Which sequence matches the lecture's integrated pharmacology pathway?
why: One integrated pathway: Dose → Absorption → Distribution → Receptor/Target → Effect, with Metabolism and Excretion clearing the drug.

whys.A: Excretion clears the drug; it doesn't deliver it.
whys.B: The drug must be absorbed and distributed before reaching the target.
whys.D: Absorption comes before distribution.
whys.E: Metabolism and excretion are the clearing steps.

takeaway: Use the pathway as your checklist for any drug.
discriminator: Delivery (A, D) comes before the target; clearance (M, E) removes drug.

stem: Which target class directly gates the flow of ions across a membrane?
why: Ion channels directly gate the flow of ions across a membrane.

whys.A: Drugs inhibit or, less commonly, activate enzyme activity.
whys.C: Nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) are targets for some antimicrobials and gene therapies.
whys.D: Nuclear receptors are a receptor subtype, not ion gates.
whys.E: Transporters are carrier proteins that move substances.

takeaway: Receptors include ligand-gated ion channels, but the ion channel class itself gates ion flow.
discriminator: Gating ions → ion channels; carrying substances → transporters.

stem: A PA counsels a patient who buys several brand-name and store-brand products. Why should the PA prescribe and counsel by generic name?

options.B: Generic names are the marketed trade names
options.C: Generic names are unambiguous and international
options.D: Generic names describe the exact structure
options.E: Generic names differ for each manufacturer

why: Generic names are unambiguous and international, avoiding confusion when one ingredient hides under multiple brand names.

whys.A: BRAND names change between countries; generic names do not.
whys.B: Marketed trade names are brand names.
whys.D: That is the chemical name.
whys.E: There is one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.

takeaway: Generic = one official non-proprietary name per drug.
discriminator: Brand varies by maker and country; generic does not.

stem: A PA must adjust a renally cleared drug for a patient with CKD. Which bedside estimates of renal function guide the adjustment?
why: eGFR and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard bedside estimates of renal function used to adjust dosing.

whys.A: These are PK measures, not renal function estimates.
whys.B: These are pharmacogenomic tests.
whys.D: These describe distribution and potency.
whys.E: These describe absorption.

takeaway: Renal dosing is guided by eGFR/CrCl.
discriminator: Renal function → eGFR/CrCl; genetics → TPMT/CYP tests.

stem: An IV dose gives 100 mg/L; the half-life is 6 hours. What is the concentration at 18 hours?
why: 18 h = 3 half-lives: C(t) = 100 x (1/2)^3 = 12.5 mg/L (87.5% eliminated).

whys.A: That is at 12 hours (2 half-lives).
whys.C: That is at 6 hours (1 half-life).
whys.D: That is at 24 hours (4 half-lives).
whys.E: That is at 30 hours (5 half-lives).

takeaway: Count half-lives first, then halve.
discriminator: Divide elapsed time by t½ to get the number of halvings.

stem: Monoclonal antibodies and gene- or cell-based therapies belong to which source of new drugs?
why: Biologics = monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.

whys.B: Natural products come from plants, fungi, microbes, and marine organisms.
whys.C: Repurposing finds a new use for an already approved drug.
whys.D: Surveillance is a regulatory phase, not a drug source.
whys.E: Synthetic sources are designed small molecules (and recombinant proteins via biotech).

takeaway: Four sources: natural products, synthetic & biotech, biologics, repurposing.
discriminator: Antibodies and gene/cell therapies → biologics.

stem: Which drug did the lecture use as an example of a very high Vd?
why: Digoxin has a very high Vd — it is mostly sequestered in tissue, not floating around in plasma.

whys.B: Albuterol was the β2-agonist example.
whys.C: Morphine was named for first-pass effect.
whys.D: Lithium was named for narrow TI and renal clearance.
whys.E: Heparin was named for the subcutaneous route.

takeaway: Digoxin: high Vd AND narrow TI.
discriminator: Digoxin appears in both the Vd and narrow-TI lists.

stem: Which chain correctly orders the pharmacodynamic pathway?
why: Drug → target → signal transduction → response; every PD topic maps onto this chain.

whys.A: The drug binds the target first; signaling then produces the response.
whys.C: The target and signaling come before the response.
whys.D: Absorption and excretion are PK, not the PD pathway.
whys.E: Binding to the target starts signal transduction.

takeaway: Write the chain: drug, target, signal, response.
discriminator: PD chains describe binding and signaling — not ADME steps.

stem: Which is the dominant elimination route for most drugs and their metabolites?
why: The kidney is the dominant route for most drugs and metabolites.

whys.A: A minor route.
whys.B: Minor, but matters for lactating patients.
whys.C: For volatile agents (anesthetic gases).
whys.E: Important for some large or protein-bound drugs.

takeaway: Kidney first; bile for large/protein-bound drugs.
discriminator: Lungs = volatile agents; breast milk = lactation concern.

stem: How is the therapeutic index calculated?
why: Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).

whys.B: Emax is efficacy; TI uses the toxic dose.
whys.C: EC₅₀ and Emax describe potency and efficacy, not TI.
whys.D: TI is a ratio, not a difference.
whys.E: Reversed — the toxic dose goes on top.

takeaway: TI = Toxic over Effective.
discriminator: Bigger TI = wider safety margin.

stem: How is clearance defined?

options.B: Time for plasma level to fall by half
options.C: Fraction of a dose reaching circulation
options.D: Plasma volume fully cleared of drug per time
options.E: Total drug relative to plasma level

why: Clearance = the volume of plasma from which drug is completely removed per unit time.

whys.A: That is steady state.
whys.B: That is half-life.
whys.C: That is bioavailability.
whys.E: That is volume of distribution.

takeaway: Clearance is a VOLUME per TIME.
discriminator: Half-life is time; Vd is volume; clearance is volume per time.

stem: A patient is starting clopidogrel. Variation in which gene affects its activation?
why: CYP2C19 variation affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing.

whys.A: CYP3A4 was used for the interaction example.
whys.B: TPMT affects thiopurine toxicity.
whys.C: CYP2D6 affects codeine activation.
whys.E: HLA-B*5801 affects allopurinol reactions.

takeaway: CYP2C19 → Clopidogrel.
discriminator: Both CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 involve activation — match the drug.

stem: Which sequence describes the first-pass route of an oral drug?

options.A: GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic
options.B: GI tract → systemic → liver → portal circulation
options.C: GI tract → portal circulation → systemic → liver
options.D: GI tract → kidney → portal circulation → systemic
options.E: GI tract → liver → portal circulation → systemic

why: Oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.

whys.B: First-pass happens BEFORE systemic circulation.
whys.C: The liver comes before systemic circulation.
whys.D: The kidney is not on the first-pass path.
whys.E: Portal circulation carries the drug TO the liver.

takeaway: The liver gets the first pass before the body does.
discriminator: Portal vein → liver → THEN systemic circulation.

stem: Which parameters are loading and maintenance doses based on?

options.B: Loading on Vd; maintenance on clearance
options.D: Loading on bioavailability; maintenance on Vd
options.E: Loading on clearance; maintenance on Vd

why: Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance.

whys.A: Loading doses are based on Vd.
whys.C: The lecture pairs loading with Vd and maintenance with clearance.
whys.D: Loading = Vd; maintenance = clearance.
whys.E: Reversed.

takeaway: Loading → Liters (Vd); Maintenance → Moving out (clearance).
discriminator: Fill the volume first, then replace what is cleared.

stem: Which statement about pharmacologic and therapeutic effects is correct?

options.A: They are two words for the same thing
options.C: A therapeutic effect need not be measurable
options.D: Therapeutic effects occur only above range
options.E: A pharmacologic effect may not be therapeutic

why: A drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic — that is often exactly what an adverse effect is.

whys.A: The lecture stresses they are NOT synonyms.
whys.B: Only the therapeutic effect is intended; others may be adverse.
whys.C: A therapeutic effect is a pharmacologic effect — a measurable change.
whys.D: Harm above the range is toxicity, not therapeutic effect.

takeaway: Therapeutic effect = the intended, beneficial subset of pharmacologic effects.
discriminator: Pharmacologic = any measurable change; therapeutic = the intended one.

stem: A PA wants a patient's drug to avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism. Which route enters systemic venous circulation directly?

options.E: Oral, taken on an empty stomach

why: Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism.

whys.A: Food does not change the portal route.
whys.B: Any oral form is absorbed into the portal circulation.
whys.C: Crushing doesn't avoid the portal circulation.
whys.E: All oral doses go GI → portal circulation → liver first.

takeaway: Sublingual and IV bypass first-pass.
discriminator: Any swallowed form still meets the liver first.

stem: Which organs receive a drug fastest during distribution?
why: Highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).

whys.A: Bone and fat are poorly perfused.
whys.B: Only the heart here is highly perfused.
whys.C: Fat is poorly perfused; the listed fast organs are brain, heart, kidney.
whys.D: Fat and bone are poorly perfused and receive drug slowly.

takeaway: Perfusion drives early distribution.
discriminator: Fast: brain, heart, kidney. Slow: fat, bone.

stem: A patient's eGFR drops with new CKD. How should a primarily renally eliminated drug be adjusted?

options.C: Make no adjustment to dose or interval
options.D: Raise the dose to maintain the effect
options.E: Lower the dose and/or extend the interval

why: Reduced renal clearance raises exposure; respond with a lower dose, a longer interval, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl.

whys.A: Route doesn't fix reduced renal clearance.
whys.B: Intervals are EXTENDED in renal impairment.
whys.C: Reduced renal function raises exposure.
whys.D: That worsens accumulation.

takeaway: CKD: less drug, less often.
discriminator: Extend intervals — never shorten them — when clearance falls.

stem: A patient inhales albuterol and the airways open within minutes. Which sequence explains this?

options.A: β2 blockade → ↓ cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.B: β2 activation → ↓ cAMP → smooth muscle contraction
options.C: β2 activation → ↑ cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation

why: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: β2 activation → increased intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxation → bronchodilation.

whys.A: Albuterol is a β2 AGONIST; cAMP rises.
whys.B: cAMP rises and muscle relaxes.
whys.D: The mechanism is receptor activation with rising cAMP.
whys.E: Albuterol acts on the β2 receptor and causes relaxation.

takeaway: Receptor → second messenger → effect: β2 → cAMP → relaxation.
discriminator: Agonist = activates; cAMP goes UP; airway muscle RELAXES.

stem: Two drugs treat the same symptom. Drug A works at 5 mg; Drug B needs 50 mg but reaches a higher maximal effect. Which matters more for choice?
why: Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.

whys.A: Drug B reaches a higher maximal effect — that matters.
whys.B: A smaller dose means greater POTENCY, not efficacy.
whys.D: Potency matters for dosing, not for picking the 'better' drug.
whys.E: Higher Emax = more efficacious, not more potent.

takeaway: Choose by efficacy (Emax); dose by potency.
discriminator: Potency tells you HOW MUCH to give; efficacy tells you HOW WELL it can work.
src: L01 S34; S34 (notes); L02 S48; SG U1-R6

stem: Which two parameters together determine half-life?
why: Half-life is determined by clearance and Vd together — not a fixed drug property independent of physiology.

whys.B: TI is a safety margin, not a PK determinant.
whys.C: These describe absorption and PD.
whys.D: Half-life is not set by dose or route.
whys.E: Vd, not bioavailability, pairs with clearance.

takeaway: t½ depends on clearance + Vd.
discriminator: Change clearance (e.g., CKD) and half-life changes.

stem: In the lecture's figure, an inhibitor raises a substrate to 240% of baseline and an inducer lowers it to 42%. Which poses toxicity risk?

options.A: Neither, since both are within range
options.B: The inducer, lowering the level to 42%
options.C: The inhibitor, raising the level to 240%
options.D: Both equally, since any change is toxic
options.E: Baseline, since it is the reference level

why: The inhibitor bar (240%) shows the substrate accumulating because it can't be cleared normally; the inducer (42%) risks failure instead.

whys.A: 240% of baseline is far above baseline.
whys.B: Falling levels risk therapeutic failure, not toxicity.
whys.D: Only the rising level raises toxicity risk.
whys.E: Baseline is the comparison point, not the risk.

takeaway: Above 100% = toxicity risk; below 100% = failure risk.
discriminator: Direction of change tells you the risk.

stem: Two years after approval, a serious reaction appears in about 1 in 10,000 patients. Why was it missed earlier?

options.A: Approval occurs before any human trials
options.B: Phase III never monitors any adverse effects
options.C: Trials were too small and short to detect it
options.D: Phase I enrolled patients with the condition
options.E: Reporting systems accept only voluntary reports

why: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trials are too small and too short to catch 1-in-10,000 events.

whys.A: Approval follows clinical trials and FDA review.
whys.B: Phase III confirms efficacy AND monitors adverse effects at scale.
whys.D: Phase I enrolls healthy volunteers.
whys.E: Reporting is both voluntary and mandatory.

takeaway: Phase IV (postmarketing) is where rare adverse effects surface.
discriminator: Rare + after approval → Phase IV surveillance caught what trials could not.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24) starts a narrow-TI antiarrhythmic eliminated unchanged by the kidney; she began a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor 3 weeks ago. What is the FIRST concern?

options.A: Reduced renal clearance shortening the half-life
options.B: CYP3A4 induction lowering the antiarrhythmic level
options.C: Increased Vd from her advanced kidney disease
options.E: Reduced renal clearance raising level and half-life

why: CKD reduces renal clearance, raising the drug's concentration and prolonging its half-life regardless of the new drug.

whys.A: Lower clearance PROLONGS half-life.
whys.B: She takes an INHIBITOR, and inducers lower levels.
whys.C: The study guide focuses on clearance, not Vd.
whys.D: Not the concern raised for this case.

takeaway: Renally eliminated drug + low eGFR = accumulation risk.
discriminator: Concern 1 is renal (independent of the CYP drug); concern 2 is the CYP3A4 inhibitor.

stem: A patient overdoses on acetaminophen, and normal Phase I metabolism produces NAPQI. What is NAPQI an example of?

options.A: A prodrug activated by Phase II
options.C: An efflux pump at the blood-brain barrier
options.E: A toxic metabolite from normal metabolism

why: NAPQI (from acetaminophen) is the textbook example of a toxic metabolite produced by normal Phase I metabolism.

whys.A: NAPQI is produced by Phase I, and it is toxic.
whys.B: It is a toxic metabolite, not an inactive conjugate.
whys.C: That is P-glycoprotein.
whys.D: It is a metabolite of acetaminophen, not an inhibitor.

takeaway: Metabolism can make a drug toxic, not only inactive.
discriminator: NAPQI = toxic metabolite of acetaminophen via Phase I.

stem: Which name describes a drug's exact molecular structure?
why: The chemical name describes the exact molecular structure and is rarely used in clinical practice.

whys.A: Store brands are marketed names (e.g., for acetaminophen).
whys.C: Brand = the manufacturer's marketed name.
whys.D: Trade name is another term for brand name.
whys.E: Generic = the official, non-proprietary name of the active drug.

takeaway: Chemical = structure; generic = official name; brand = marketed name.
discriminator: Only the chemical name encodes structure — and it's rarely used clinically.

stem: A breastfeeding patient asks about a new drug. Why does breast milk, a minor elimination route, still matter here?

options.B: It traps ionized drug in urine
options.D: It is the dominant route for most drugs

why: Sweat and breast milk are minor routes, but breast milk matters for lactating patients.

whys.B: Ion trapping happens in the renal tubule.
whys.C: Bile/feces handle large or protein-bound drugs.
whys.D: The kidney is dominant.
whys.E: The lungs clear volatile agents.

takeaway: Minor route, major relevance in lactation.
discriminator: Lactation turns a minor route into a safety question.

stem: A patient takes a drug that is highly bound to plasma proteins. Which fraction of it is active and able to cross membranes?
why: Only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.

whys.A: Polar drugs cross membranes poorly.
whys.C: Bound drug is not active and cannot cross membranes.
whys.D: Conjugation makes a water-soluble product for excretion.
whys.E: Fatty-tissue drug is distributed, not the active plasma fraction.

takeaway: Free drug acts; bound drug waits.
discriminator: Protein binding lowers the active fraction.

stem: A PA starts lithium. Compared with a wide-TI drug, what does lithium's narrow TI mean for care?

options.A: Skip levels since IV is fully bioavailable
options.B: Skip monitoring since the margin is wide
options.C: Use lower doses since Emax is higher
options.D: Dose freely since potency is high
options.E: Dose carefully and monitor blood levels

why: Narrow TI: effective and toxic doses are close — careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.

whys.A: Bioavailability is unrelated to the narrow-TI monitoring need.
whys.B: A NARROW TI means a small margin — monitoring is needed.
whys.C: TI is about toxic vs. effective doses, not Emax.
whys.D: Potency is about dose size, not the safety margin.

takeaway: Narrow-TI drugs need therapeutic drug monitoring.
discriminator: Small dosing errors can move a narrow-TI patient from effective to toxic.

stem: A new drug weakens a patient's home medication at the same receptor; raising the home dose restores the full effect. What is the new drug?
why: A competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — restoring the effect supports competitive rather than irreversible antagonism.

whys.A: Noncompetitive antagonists reduce Emax, which more agonist can't restore.
whys.B: The described behavior is blockade overcome by more agonist.
whys.D: Inverse agonists lower baseline activity; the scenario shows surmountable blockade.
whys.E: Irreversible antagonism would not be overcome by raising the dose.

takeaway: Surmountable blockade = competitive antagonism.
discriminator: Effect restored by more agonist → competitive; not restored → irreversible/noncompetitive.
src: L02 S41; L01 S22; SG U1-M

stem: A healthy 25-year-old volunteer joins a small study testing a new drug's safety, tolerability, and dosing. Which phase is this?
why: Phase I = safety, tolerability, dose-finding in a small group of healthy volunteers.

whys.A: Phase III confirms efficacy at scale in hundreds to thousands of patients.
whys.B: Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval.
whys.C: Preclinical testing comes before any human trial.
whys.D: Phase II gives preliminary efficacy in a few hundred PATIENTS with the condition.

takeaway: Per the slides, Phase I is the healthy-volunteer phase (textbook: 20–100 people; very toxic drugs, e.g., cancer, are tested in patients instead, p. 17).
discriminator: Healthy volunteers → Phase I; patients with the condition → Phase II onward.

stem: About what percentage of the original concentration remains after 3 half-lives?
why: Each half-life halves what remains: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5% after 3 t½.

whys.A: About 3% remains after 5 half-lives.
whys.C: 50% remains after 1 half-life.
whys.D: 25% remains after 2 half-lives.
whys.E: 6.25% remains after 4 half-lives.

takeaway: % remaining = 100% x (1/2)^n.
discriminator: Remaining vs. eliminated: 12.5% remains = 87.5% eliminated.

stem: Which drugs did the lecture name as having a large first-pass effect?
why: Large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all need higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) for the same exposure as IV.

whys.A: Warfarin was named as narrow-TI, not first-pass.
whys.C: Albuterol was the β2 agonist example.
whys.D: Digoxin was named for narrow TI and high Vd.
whys.E: Lithium was named as narrow-TI.

takeaway: "Need Plenty More by mouth": Nitroglycerin, Propranolol, Morphine.
discriminator: First-pass list ≠ narrow-TI list.

stem: For the same patient (stage 4 CKD, narrow-TI renally cleared antiarrhythmic, CYP3A4 inhibitor), what should happen before dispensing?

options.A: Check eGFR/CrCl, reduce dose or extend interval
options.B: Shorten the interval to reach steady state faster
options.C: Raise the dose to offset the CYP3A4 inhibitor
options.D: Stop all monitoring since the drug is oral
options.E: Give the standard dose and recheck labs in a year

why: Before dispensing: check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and monitor renal function and signs of toxicity closely after starting.

whys.B: Intervals are extended in renal impairment.
whys.C: An inhibitor RAISES levels; raising the dose adds risk.
whys.D: Route doesn't remove the need for monitoring.
whys.E: Exposure is already increased; adjust and monitor closely.

takeaway: Adjust first, then monitor closely.
discriminator: CKD + narrow TI + inhibitor → lower/longer dosing + close monitoring.

stem: A patient takes twice the prescribed dose; serum levels rise above the therapeutic range and harm follows. What is this?
why: Toxicity = harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.

whys.A: Induction LOWERS substrate levels.
whys.B: A therapeutic effect is intended and beneficial.
whys.C: An ADR occurs at NORMAL therapeutic doses.
whys.E: That is a receptor concept, not a dosing harm.

takeaway: Above the range → toxicity; at normal dose → ADR.
discriminator: The level relative to the therapeutic range decides the term.

stem: A patient is prescribed an older, already-approved drug for a condition it was recently found to treat. Which source of new drugs is this?
why: Drug repurposing = an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.

whys.A: Biologics are antibodies and gene- or cell-based therapies.
whys.B: These are designed small molecules and recombinant proteins.
whys.C: Surveillance monitors safety; it isn't a drug source.
whys.D: Natural products come from plants, fungi, microbes, marine organisms.

takeaway: Old drug + new use = repurposing.
discriminator: 'Already approved' is the clue for repurposing.

stem: Why are CYP450 interactions considered one of the highest-yield concepts?

options.A: They cannot be predicted before prescribing
options.B: They affect only the IV route of dosing
options.C: Nearly every drug class has an important one
options.D: They occur only with narrow-TI drugs
options.E: They are limited to Phase II metabolism

why: Nearly every major drug class has at least one clinically important CYP interaction.

whys.A: They are predictable and preventable.
whys.B: Route doesn't limit CYP interactions.
whys.D: They occur widely; narrow TI makes them more dangerous.
whys.E: CYP450 is Phase I.

takeaway: CYP interactions are everywhere — screen every time.
discriminator: Predictable + common = high-yield.

stem: Which renal process reduces a drug's net elimination?
why: Tubular reabsorption: lipophilic, un-ionized drug passively diffuses back into the blood, reducing net elimination.

whys.B: Filtration moves drug INTO the tubule.
whys.C: Secretion moves more drug INTO the tubule.
whys.D: Lung elimination is not renal.
whys.E: That is filtration, which adds drug to the tubule.

takeaway: Reabsorption works against elimination.
discriminator: Only the un-ionized, lipophilic form diffuses back.

stem: Drug X needs a lower dose than Drug Y for the same effect; both reach the same Emax. Which is true?

options.A: X has the narrower therapeutic index
options.B: X is more potent and more efficacious
options.C: Y is more potent; efficacy is equal
options.D: X is more efficacious; potency is equal
options.E: X is more potent; efficacy is equal

why: Lower dose for the same effect = greater potency; same Emax = equal efficacy. Potency and efficacy are independent.

whys.A: No toxic-dose data are given; TI = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀.
whys.B: Same Emax → efficacy is the same.
whys.C: The drug needing the LOWER dose (X) is more potent.
whys.D: Equal Emax means equal efficacy; lower dose means greater potency.

takeaway: Potency = dose needed (EC₅₀); efficacy = ceiling (Emax).
discriminator: Same ceiling → only potency differs.

stem: A critically ill patient needs immediate drug onset with no absorption phase. Which route fits?
why: IV: 100% bioavailable, immediate onset, no absorption phase.

whys.A: Sublingual is absorbed into systemic circulation — still an absorption step.
whys.B: IM is faster than oral but still has absorption.
whys.C: SC gives slower, steady absorption.
whys.D: Transdermal is slow and sustained.

takeaway: IV = no absorption step at all.
discriminator: Every other route has some absorption phase.

stem: Which statement correctly pairs each branch with its question?

options.A: PK: body acts on drug; PD: drug acts on body
options.B: PK: drug acts on body; PD: body acts on drug
options.C: PK: drug development stages; PD: postmarketing safety signals
options.D: PK: receptor binding and effect; PD: absorption and excretion
options.E: PK: genetic variation in response; PD: poisoning and overdose

why: Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME); pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect).

whys.B: Reversed — PK is the body acting on the drug (ADME).
whys.C: Development and surveillance are regulation topics, not PK/PD.
whys.D: Receptors & effect are PD; ADME is PK.
whys.E: Those are pharmacogenomics and toxicology.

takeaway: PK = body → drug (ADME). PD = drug → body (receptors, potency, efficacy).
discriminator: If the question is about movement (absorbed, distributed, cleared) it's PK; if about binding or effect size it's PD.
src: L01 S6; SG U1-R1; L02 S44

stem: Which four drugs did the lecture name as classic narrow-therapeutic-index drugs?
why: Classic narrow-TI drugs: warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin — each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.

whys.A: Morphine was named for first-pass effect.
whys.B: Albuterol was the β2-agonist example.
whys.D: Heparin was named as a subcutaneous drug, not narrow TI.
whys.E: Propranolol was named for first-pass effect, not narrow TI.

takeaway: "Watch Levels During Prescribing": Warfarin, Lithium, Digoxin, Phenytoin.
discriminator: Propranolol, morphine, nitroglycerin = first-pass list; don't mix the lists.

stem: According to the course study guide, which factor can ALSO lower real-world effectiveness below trial efficacy?

options.A: Strict adherence to the dosing schedule
options.B: Enrollment of healthy Phase I volunteers
options.C: Use of the IV route instead of oral
options.E: Higher potency than the trial drug

why: The study guide adds that adherence, comorbidities, AND interactions can all reduce effectiveness below trial efficacy.

whys.A: Good adherence would support, not reduce, effectiveness.
whys.B: Phase I enrollment has no bearing on clinic effectiveness.
whys.C: IV gives 100% bioavailability; route is not the listed factor.
whys.E: Potency affects dosing, not effectiveness in practice.

takeaway: Real-world effectiveness: adherence, comorbidities, interactions.
discriminator: The slides list adherence and comorbidities; the study guide adds interactions.

stem: What is the main result of Phase II conjugation?

options.A: Activation of a prodrug by CYP450 enzymes
options.B: A more water-soluble product for excretion
options.C: A more lipophilic product for reabsorption
options.D: Unmasking of a reactive functional group
options.E: A larger Vd from tissue sequestration

why: Phase II attaches a polar group, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion.

whys.A: CYP450 activity is Phase I.
whys.C: Phase II attaches a POLAR group → water-soluble.
whys.D: That describes Phase I.
whys.E: Phase II targets excretion, not Vd.

takeaway: Phase II = tag it → water-soluble → excrete.
discriminator: Phase I unmasks; Phase II conjugates.

stem: Which item is NOT on the lecture's before-you-prescribe checklist?
why: Checklist: indication; contraindications and allergies; renal and hepatic function; drug interactions (incl. CYP450); age, pregnancy, patient factors; correct dose, route, and monitoring plan.

whys.A: Listed.
whys.B: Listed.
whys.C: Listed.
whys.E: Listed.

takeaway: Memorize the six-item checklist.
discriminator: Names don't appear on the safety checklist; organ function and interactions do.

stem: Which antagonist permanently inactivates its receptor until new receptor is synthesized?
why: Irreversible antagonist = permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.

whys.B: Competitive antagonists bind reversibly and are surmountable.
whys.C: Noncompetitive = binds elsewhere or irreversibly; 'until resynthesis' defines irreversible.
whys.D: Inverse agonists lower baseline activity; they don't destroy receptors.
whys.E: Partial agonists activate submaximally.

takeaway: Irreversible effects last until new receptor is made.
discriminator: 'Until new receptor is synthesized' is the irreversible signature.

stem: A patient with meningitis receives a highly polar antibiotic. How does this drug reach the CNS?

options.A: Easily, since tight junctions favor polar drugs
options.B: Easily, since the brain is poorly perfused
options.C: Easily, since P-glycoprotein pumps it inward
options.D: Poorly normally, better with inflamed meninges
options.E: Never, even when the meninges are inflamed

why: A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.

whys.A: Tight junctions restrict paracellular movement.
whys.B: The brain is highly perfused; the BBB is the barrier.
whys.C: P-gp pumps drugs OUT of the CNS.
whys.E: Inflamed meninges are the stated exception.

takeaway: Inflamed meninges let polar drugs in.
discriminator: Polar = poor BBB entry, except in meningitis.

stem: A patient starts a regularly dosed medication with no loading dose. About how many half-lives until steady state?
why: Steady state — intake equals elimination — is reached in roughly 4–5 half-lives, regardless of dose size.

whys.A: Too many.
whys.B: Too few.
whys.D: Too few.
whys.E: That describes a loading dose reaching target.

takeaway: Steady state ≈ 4–5 half-lives.
discriminator: "Five to fill, five to empty."

stem: A patient with worsening renal impairment takes several medicines. Which renally cleared, narrow-TI drugs did the lecture flag for adjustment?
why: Any renally-cleared, narrow-TI drug (many antibiotics, digoxin, lithium) needs a dose or interval adjustment in renal impairment.

whys.A: Morphine was named for first-pass effect.
whys.C: Heparin was named for the SC route.
whys.D: Albuterol was the β2-agonist example.
whys.E: Propranolol was named for first-pass effect.

takeaway: Renal + narrow TI: antibiotics, digoxin, lithium.
discriminator: Digoxin and lithium sit on both the narrow-TI and renal lists.

stem: Drug A, a CYP inducer, is started in a patient on Drug B, a substrate of that enzyme. What happens to Drug B?

options.A: Its level is unchanged by enzyme induction
options.B: Its level rises, raising toxicity risk
options.C: Its elimination route shifts to biliary
options.D: Its level falls, risking therapeutic failure
options.E: Its level rises, then falls to baseline

why: Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.

whys.A: Induction lowers substrate levels.
whys.B: Rising levels follow an INHIBITOR.
whys.C: Induction changes the rate, not the route.
whys.E: Induction lowers, not raises, the level.

takeaway: Inducer → substrate ↓ → therapeutic failure.
discriminator: Inhibitor = toxicity risk; inducer = failure risk.

stem: A patient needs a therapeutic drug level right away, so a loading dose is added. What is the clinical advantage?

options.A: Shortening the drug's half-life for good
options.B: Removing the need for drug-level monitoring
options.C: No real advantage over maintenance alone
options.E: Reaching target immediately, not after 4–5 t½

why: A loading dose reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives.

whys.A: Half-life is set by clearance and Vd.
whys.B: Monitoring is still needed.
whys.C: It reaches the target right away.
whys.D: A loading dose doesn't change the maintenance dose.

takeaway: Loading dose = skip the wait.
discriminator: It changes the start, not the maintenance dose or monitoring.

stem: A patient receives a drug that occupies every one of its receptors yet produces only a submaximal response. What is the drug?
why: Partial agonist = submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.

whys.A: An antagonist blocks the agonist; it doesn't partially activate.
whys.B: An inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal.
whys.C: A full agonist produces maximal activation.
whys.E: Irreversible antagonists inactivate receptors until new ones are made.

takeaway: Full occupancy but submaximal response defines a partial agonist.
discriminator: 'Even at full occupancy' separates partial agonist from a full agonist at low dose.

stem: A patient on a standard dose with levels inside the therapeutic range develops an unintended, harmful reaction. What is this?
why: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.

whys.A: Toxicity is harm when dose/exposure EXCEEDS the therapeutic range; levels here are in range.
whys.B: First-pass is hepatic metabolism of oral drug before systemic circulation.
whys.C: That is a receptor interaction, not a type of adverse event.
whys.E: A therapeutic effect is intended and beneficial.

takeaway: ADR = harm at normal doses; toxicity = harm above the therapeutic range.
discriminator: Check the dose/level: in range → ADR; above range → toxicity.

stem: Which renal process passes free drug from blood into the tubule based on molecular size?
why: Glomerular filtration: free (unbound) drug passes from blood into the tubule based on molecular size.

whys.A: Biliary excretion is not a renal process.
whys.B: Conjugation is Phase II metabolism.
whys.D: Secretion uses active transporters.
whys.E: Reabsorption moves drug back into the blood.

takeaway: Filtration = free drug, by size.
discriminator: Size-based → filtration; transporter-based → secretion.

stem: If that antiarrhythmic were cleared mainly by hepatic CYP3A4 instead of the kidney, which concern would dominate?
why: If hepatically/CYP3A4 cleared, the renal concern is less central (CKD can still indirectly affect hepatic handling), and the CYP3A4 interaction becomes dominant.

whys.A: TPMT relates to thiopurines.
whys.B: It becomes less central if clearance is hepatic.
whys.D: HLA relates to hypersensitivity (e.g., allopurinol).
whys.E: Not the concern described.

takeaway: Clearance route decides which risk dominates.
discriminator: Renal drug → CKD dominates; CYP3A4 drug → inhibitor dominates.

stem: Which chain correctly follows reduced renal clearance?

options.A: t½ unchanged → time to steady state unchanged → none
options.B: t½ ↑ → time to steady state ↓ → accumulation
options.C: t½ ↓ → time to steady state ↑ → failure
options.D: t½ ↓ → time to steady state ↓ → accumulation
options.E: t½ ↑ → time to steady state ↑ → accumulation

why: Clearance down → half-life up → time to steady state up → accumulation risk up if the regimen isn't adjusted.

whys.A: Half-life depends on clearance.
whys.B: Longer half-life means LONGER time to steady state.
whys.C: Half-life rises, and the risk is accumulation.
whys.D: Half-life RISES when clearance falls.

takeaway: Walk the chain: clearance, half-life, steady-state time, accumulation.
discriminator: Every step after clearance moves UP.

stem: With no agonist present, a drug lowers a receptor's baseline activity below normal. What is it?
why: An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal.

whys.B: Noncompetitive antagonists lower the agonist's Emax, not baseline.
whys.C: A full agonist produces maximal activation.
whys.D: Partial agonists produce submaximal ACTIVATION.
whys.E: A true antagonist blocks the agonist without lowering baseline itself.

takeaway: Below baseline with no agonist = inverse agonist.
discriminator: Antagonists need an agonist to block; inverse agonists act on their own.

stem: A patient is prescribed codeine. Variation in which enzyme alters codeine activation (and many antidepressants)?
why: CYP2D6 variation alters metabolism of many antidepressants and opioids (e.g., codeine activation).

whys.A: CYP3A4 was the inhibitor/substrate interaction example.
whys.C: HLA-B*5801 affects allopurinol hypersensitivity.
whys.D: CYP2C19 affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing.
whys.E: TPMT affects thiopurine toxicity.

takeaway: CYP2D6 → codeine.
discriminator: Codeine needs activation — CYP2D6 does it.

stem: A PA needs a drug to reach a patient's central nervous system. Which drug properties favor crossing the blood-brain barrier?
why: Small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross the BBB more easily than large, polar, or highly protein-bound drugs.

whys.A: Polar and protein-bound drugs cross poorly.
whys.B: Ionized and protein-bound drugs cross poorly.
whys.D: Large drugs cross less easily.
whys.E: These properties cross the BBB poorly.

takeaway: Small + lipophilic + non-ionized = gets into the CNS.
discriminator: Any of large/polar/bound slows BBB entry.

stem: A patient is switched from an IV to an oral form of the same drug, and less of each dose now reaches the circulation. Which branch describes this change?

options.B: Pharmacodynamics, because it concerns receptor binding
options.C: Pharmacogenomics, because it concerns genetic variation
options.D: Toxicology, because it concerns poisoning risk
options.E: Pharmacodynamics, because it concerns drug effect

why: Bioavailability is the fraction of a dose reaching systemic circulation — an absorption (ADME) property, so it is pharmacokinetics.

whys.B: Receptor binding is PD; bioavailability is the fraction reaching circulation (PK).
whys.C: Nothing genetic is described; the route changed.
whys.D: Toxicology studies poisoning; this is an ADME change.
whys.E: Effect size at the receptor is PD; bioavailability is about how much drug arrives — PK.

takeaway: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion all belong to PK.
discriminator: Ask: is the body handling the drug (PK) or is the drug acting on the body (PD)?

stem: Which statement about routes and first-pass metabolism matches the lecture?

options.B: IM and SC undergo first-pass like oral
options.C: Essentially every route except oral bypasses it
options.D: Only the IV route bypasses first-pass

why: Routes that bypass first-pass: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.

whys.A: Only the oral route goes through the portal circulation first.
whys.B: IM and SC bypass first-pass.
whys.D: Sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, and IM also bypass it.
whys.E: Transdermal is listed among routes that bypass first-pass.

takeaway: Per the lecture, oral is the route that meets first-pass metabolism (textbook: rectal is partly subject to it too, p. 48–49).
discriminator: If it isn't swallowed, it skips the portal first pass.

stem: On a dose-response curve, what does EC₅₀ measure?

options.A: Toxicity — the dose harming 50% of patients
options.D: Safety — the gap between effect and harm

why: EC₅₀ = the concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.

whys.A: That would be TD₅₀, used in the therapeutic index.
whys.C: Emax (the plateau) measures efficacy.
whys.D: That gap is the therapeutic index.
whys.E: Bioavailability (F) is a PK parameter.

takeaway: Lower EC₅₀ = more potent.
discriminator: EC₅₀ sits halfway up the curve on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau.

stem: A patient will inject insulin at home. Which route did the lecture describe as slower, steady absorption, common for insulin and heparin?
why: Subcutaneous (SC): slower, steady absorption; common for insulin, heparin.

whys.A: Inhaled gives a rapid local effect in the lungs.
whys.B: Transdermal is slow, sustained absorption through the skin.
whys.C: Sublingual goes directly into systemic circulation.
whys.D: IM is faster than oral and good for depot formulations.

takeaway: SC = insulin, heparin.
discriminator: IM = depot/long-acting; SC = steady (insulin, heparin).

stem: Which definition matches toxicity as taught in this unit?

options.A: Harm that occurs at normal therapeutic doses only
options.B: The intended, beneficial effect for a condition
options.C: Loss of effect after a CYP inducer is added
options.D: Any measurable biological change a drug produces
options.E: Harm as dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range

why: Toxicity = harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.

whys.A: That is an adverse drug reaction (ADR).
whys.B: That is a therapeutic effect.
whys.C: That is induction-related therapeutic failure.
whys.D: That is a pharmacologic effect.

takeaway: Toxicity is dose-driven harm beyond the therapeutic range.
discriminator: The phrase 'exceeds the therapeutic range' separates toxicity from an ADR.

stem: After an aspirin overdose, the team alkalinizes the urine. How does this increase elimination?

options.A: It makes the drug lipophilic for reabsorption
options.B: It traps ionized drug, blocking reabsorption
options.C: It boosts filtration of protein-bound drug
options.D: It shifts elimination to bile and feces
options.E: It activates secretion by tubular transporters

why: Urine pH manipulation (alkalinizing urine in aspirin overdose) traps ionized drug in the tubule, blocking reabsorption.

whys.A: That would REDUCE elimination.
whys.C: Only free drug is filtered.
whys.D: The effect is in the renal tubule.
whys.E: Urine pH works by blocking reabsorption.

takeaway: Ionized drug stays in the urine.
discriminator: Ion trapping blocks reabsorption.

stem: A patient takes "Tylenol" for headaches and separately takes acetaminophen. What is the main risk?

options.A: A CYP3A4 interaction between two different drugs
options.B: No risk, since brand and generic names differ
options.C: Unintentional double-dosing of the same ingredient
options.D: Competitive antagonism at the same receptor site

why: Tylenol is a brand of acetaminophen; taking both doubles the dose. Check for accidental double-dosing.

whys.A: They are the same drug (acetaminophen), not two interacting drugs.
whys.B: Different names hide the same ingredient — the core risk.
whys.D: Both are the same agonist ingredient; no antagonist is involved.
whys.E: First-pass is not the issue; duplicate dosing is.

takeaway: One generic ingredient can hide under several brand names.
discriminator: Same ingredient under two names = duplicate therapy, not an interaction.

stem: A patient stable on IV propranolol switches to oral and needs a much higher dose for the same exposure. Why?

options.A: Oral propranolol cannot cross the blood-brain barrier
options.B: High protein binding inactivates the oral form
options.C: Extensive first-pass metabolism lowers oral bioavailability
options.D: A narrow therapeutic index requires higher oral doses
options.E: The IV form was less than fully bioavailable

why: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect: oral doses pass the liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV.

whys.A: BBB entry is unrelated to systemic exposure.
whys.B: Protein binding doesn't depend on the route.
whys.D: Propranolol was named for first-pass, not narrow TI.
whys.E: IV is 100% bioavailable by definition.

takeaway: Large first-pass drugs need bigger oral doses or another route.
discriminator: IV → oral dose jump = first-pass effect.

stem: A patient's drug enters the brain poorly. Which BBB structure restricts paracellular movement?

options.A: Highly perfused capillaries of the brain
options.C: Plasma proteins binding the free drug
options.E: P-glycoprotein efflux pumps in the CNS

why: Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement at the blood-brain barrier.

whys.A: Perfusion speeds delivery; it isn't the barrier.
whys.C: Protein binding limits free drug, not paracellular gaps.
whys.D: Membranes favor LIPOPHILIC drugs.
whys.E: P-gp pumps drugs OUT; it isn't the paracellular barrier.

takeaway: BBB = tight junctions + efflux pumps (P-gp).
discriminator: Tight junctions block the gaps; P-gp pumps drugs back out.

stem: Which can genetic variation alter, according to the lecture?

options.B: Only drug metabolism by CYP enzymes

why: Genetic variation can alter drug metabolism (CYP activity), transport, target structure/expression, and overall response and ADR risk.

whys.B: It also alters transport, targets, and response.
whys.C: It alters overall response, too.
whys.D: Metabolism, targets, and response are also listed.
whys.E: Genes alter the patient's handling, not the drug's structure.

takeaway: PGx touches PK (metabolism, transport) AND PD (targets).
discriminator: Watch for 'only' in pharmacogenomics options.

stem: What does P-glycoprotein do at the blood-brain barrier?

options.A: Pumps some drugs back out of the CNS
options.B: Binds free drug in the plasma permanently
options.C: Forms the tight junctions between cells
options.D: Pumps some drugs into the CNS actively
options.E: Metabolizes drugs within the brain tissue

why: Efflux transporters like P-glycoprotein can actively pump some drugs back out of the CNS.

whys.B: Plasma protein binding is a different concept.
whys.C: Tight junctions restrict paracellular movement; P-gp is a pump.
whys.D: It is an EFFLUX transporter — it pumps drugs out.
whys.E: P-gp transports; it does not metabolize.

takeaway: P-gp = efflux pump at the BBB.
discriminator: Tight junctions block; P-gp pumps out.

stem: Total clearance is usually the sum of which two components?
why: Total clearance is usually the sum of hepatic and renal clearance.

whys.A: Absorption is not clearance.
whys.B: Absorption is not clearance.
whys.C: Vd is distribution, not clearance.
whys.E: Half-life is not a clearance component.

takeaway: Total CL = hepatic + renal.
discriminator: Liver and kidney do most of the clearing.

stem: A patient stable on a narrow-TI CYP3A4 substrate starts a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What happens?

options.A: No change, since CYP3A4 is a Phase II enzyme
options.B: Substrate level rises, raising toxicity risk
options.C: Substrate level rises, lowering toxicity risk
options.D: Substrate level falls, risking therapeutic failure
options.E: Renal clearance of the substrate rises sharply

why: Inhibiting the CYP that clears the substrate slows its metabolism and raises its level — especially dangerous with a narrow TI.

whys.A: CYP450 enzymes carry out Phase I metabolism.
whys.C: Higher levels RAISE toxicity risk.
whys.D: That is the effect of an INDUCER.
whys.E: A CYP inhibitor slows metabolic clearance.

takeaway: Inhibitor → substrate ↑ → toxicity.
discriminator: Narrow TI + CYP inhibitor = high-risk combination.

stem: A drug worked in most trial patients but helps fewer patients in clinic, where doses are missed and comorbidities are common. What explains this?

options.B: The drug has a narrow therapeutic index
options.C: Potency is lower than trial potency
options.D: Effectiveness is lower than trial efficacy

why: Efficacy = performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness = everyday practice with real adherence, comorbidities (and drug interactions).

whys.A: The issue is benefit in practice, not toxicity estimates.
whys.B: TI is the effective-to-toxic margin, not real-world adherence.
whys.C: Potency is the dose needed for an effect; it doesn't explain adherence-driven gaps.
whys.E: First-pass reduces bioavailability; it isn't the real-world gap described.

takeaway: Efficacy is the trial result; effectiveness is the real-world result.
discriminator: Real-world adherence and comorbidities change effectiveness, not efficacy.

stem: Which list gives the five major drug target classes?

options.A: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, lipids, nucleic acids
options.B: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, plasma proteins
options.C: Receptors, hormones, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids
options.D: Receptors, ion channels, antibodies, transporters, nucleic acids
options.E: Receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids

why: Five target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, and nucleic acids.

whys.A: Lipids are not listed; transporters are the target class.
whys.B: Plasma proteins bind drug in distribution; nucleic acids are the 5th target.
whys.C: Hormones are not one of the five target classes; ion channels are.
whys.D: Antibodies are a biologic drug type; enzymes are the target class.

takeaway: Most drugs target receptors or enzymes.
discriminator: Ion channels and transporters matter especially for cardiac and CNS drugs.

stem: Before adding any new drug, which single check most directly prevents a predictable toxic interaction?

options.A: Review CYP450 interactions with current drugs
options.B: Review the new drug's half-life by itself
options.C: Confirm the drug's brand name with the patient
options.D: Confirm the route written on the order
options.E: Check the drug's chemical name in a reference

why: CYP450 interaction screening is one of the highest-yield steps for preventing predictable, preventable toxicity.

whys.B: Half-life alone doesn't identify interactions.
whys.C: Brand names don't screen interactions.
whys.D: Route matters, but interaction review targets this risk.
whys.E: Chemical names describe structure only.

takeaway: Always check CYP450 interactions before adding a drug.
discriminator: Interaction review — not names or half-life — prevents CYP toxicity.

stem: On log-dose curves, Drug A sits left of Drug B, and both plateau at the same height. What does this show?

options.A: A and B have different Emax values
options.B: A is more efficacious; potency is identical
options.C: B is more potent; efficacy is identical
options.D: A is more potent; efficacy is identical
options.E: A has the wider therapeutic index

why: A curve farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose (greater potency); the same plateau height means identical Emax.

whys.A: Both plateau at the same height.
whys.B: Same plateau = same efficacy; leftward = more potent.
whys.C: The curve farther LEFT (A) is more potent.
whys.E: These curves show effect only, not toxicity.

takeaway: Left shift = potency; plateau height = efficacy.
discriminator: Read the x-position for potency and the y-ceiling for efficacy.

stem: A drug relieves a chronic, non-life-threatening condition in 70% of patients but causes serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. How should a PA weigh it?

options.A: Compare it with the available alternatives
options.B: Use it only if Phase I showed no toxicity
options.C: Reject it, since any toxicity is unacceptable
options.D: Decide by its potency relative to others
options.E: Accept it, since 70% benefit outweighs any risk

why: Risk-benefit analysis is always comparative: a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if safer alternatives exist.

whys.B: Phase I safety data don't settle a postmarketing 1% risk.
whys.C: Risk-benefit is comparative, not an absolute threshold.
whys.D: Potency affects dosing, not the risk-benefit decision.
whys.E: Benefit alone isn't decisive; it depends on alternatives.

takeaway: Ask "compared to what?" rather than judging a number in isolation.
discriminator: The same risk number can be acceptable or not depending on alternatives.
